Selling a house in Fargo

No city in North Dakota has more people than Fargo, which is also the Cass County seat. It stands on the Red River's west bank, with Moorhead, Minnesota, opposite, and the combined Fargo-Moorhead metro is the state's biggest urban area. Permits and taxes depend on whether your parcel falls in Fargo, West Fargo or unincorporated Cass County, so settle that first.

The city dates to 1871. In 1893 a fire destroyed 31 downtown blocks, which were rebuilt within a year, and a tornado in 1957 flattened much of the north end. Houses in the older neighborhoods therefore differ widely from newer ones in age and construction, and buyers price that gap.

The Red River and your sale

A big part of Fargo real estate carries flood risk, which shapes insurance, lending and buyer interest. The National Weather Service measured a 1997 crest of 39.72 feet at Fargo, 2.42 feet over the 1969 record of 37.3 feet. The 2009 crest hit 40.84 feet, and the city had bought 700 houses in flood-prone areas by 2012.

The FM Area Diversion Project is meant to protect nearly 260,000 people, with permanent protection expected by 2027. Its website covers land acquisition and flood insurance status. A house near the river should be checked against the mapped floodplain, and against the diversion project's footprint, before you list.

Winters matter too. January averages 9.2 degrees Fahrenheit, about 43 days a year reach 0 or lower, and snowfall averages 51.4 inches. Roof snow load, basement moisture and heating are sensible checks before listing. If water has entered the basement, say so and share the repair records.

Rental housing inspection rules

Fargo's Inspections Department enforces the International Property Maintenance Code and Land Development Code Chapter 20 on rentals. It asks owners to record their rentals with the department at no charge. If you own a rental you plan to sell, expect a letter to the mailing address on Cass County tax records.

Inspectors look at a specific list, and a buyer's inspector will flag the same items:

  • Smoke and carbon monoxide alarms and deadbolts on entry doors
  • Stair guards, graspable handrails and peeling exterior paint
  • Bathroom and dryer ventilation, window condition and bedroom egress
  • Overcrowding, with a limit of three unrelated tenants

Owners have five business days to change a scheduled inspection date, and unanswered requests can lead to an exterior inspection and fees. The department deals with health and safety, not lease or eviction disputes.

Special assessments and what they mean for a sale

Fargo pays contractors as work is built, then pools the cost of projects about once a year and sells a Special Assessment Revenue Bond. Property owners repay it through yearly special assessment payments. Water main replacement and flood protection are examples of work funded this way. An annual installment appears on your tax statement.

To see what a parcel owes, look it up on FargoParcels.com, request a payoff amount through the city's online form, or call the Special Assessment Division at 701.241.1326. Ask the division and your title company who carries the balance at sale, and get the answer in writing before you set a closing date.

Cass County property taxes

Cass County bills real estate tax on the state schedule. Pay in full by February 15 for a 5 percent discount on the consolidated tax, or pay half plus special assessments by March 1 and the rest by October 15. Specials and drain taxes are not discounted.

Charge or eventCass County rule
First installment penalty3% on March 1, May 1, July 1 and October 15
Second installment penalty6% if unpaid after October 15
Prior-year delinquent tax1% interest per month
Tax saleThird Tuesday in November, 10:00 a.m.

All current-year property taxes must be paid in full before a deed transferring ownership can be recorded. Bills go to the owner of record as of November 1. The Finance Office is at the Cass County Courthouse, 211 9th Street South, Fargo, phone (701) 241-5600. When the house sells, the closing statement or title company settles who pays what.

What to line up before closing

Three records can hold up a Fargo closing: the mortgage payoff, the special assessment balance and the Cass County tax status. Each comes from a different office, so request them early.

  • A payoff letter from your lender
  • The special assessment payoff amount from the city's Special Assessment Division
  • Confirmation from the Cass County Finance Office that current-year taxes are paid, since the deed cannot be recorded until they are
  • Floodplain status for the parcel, and any rental inspection letters if the house has tenants

With these in hand, a cash or financed buyer can move quickly, and you can see what you will net before you commit to a date.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy Fargo houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

Ways to sell

Fargo owners can list, sell privately or accept a cash offer, and the right choice depends on the house and the timeline. A listed sale usually involves repairs, showings and a buyer's loan approval, while a cash purchase takes the house as it stands.

Whichever you pick, North Dakota's disclosure law (Century Code 47-10-02.1) requires sellers of homes with up to four units to disclose material facts, usually before final acceptance of the purchase agreement. A cash offer can be a good idea when the house needs repairs, was inherited or is a tenant-occupied rental. Compare it with listing costs and timing before you decide.

Steps from offer to closing

A Fargo sale moves through the same few steps whichever route you take. Once you accept an offer, a title company opens a file and orders the payoff figures. The lender gives a payoff letter. The Special Assessment Division gives the city balance. The Cass County Finance Office confirms that current-year taxes are paid, because the deed cannot be recorded otherwise.

Floodplain status comes up next, particularly near the river, and a rental brings inspection letters into the file. If any of these records conflict with your own, sort it out now, before the closing date, so nothing is left to clear at the table. On closing day the title company pays the lender, the city and the county from your proceeds, you sign the deed and the sale is recorded.

What a cash sale skips

A cash purchase skips the buyer's loan approval and lender appraisal, which are the two steps most likely to push a closing date back. It also skips repair negotiations, since the buyer takes the house as it stands. A house with a damp basement, an old furnace or a roof that needs work can still sell, and the cost of those problems is built into one offer.

The county and city steps do not change. Taxes, special assessments and the mortgage are still paid at closing. What changes is the number of people who must approve the deal and the time it takes. That matters if you are selling a tenant-occupied rental, settling an estate or trying to close ahead of a penalty date.

You pick the closing dateClose in as little as 7 days or on the date that works for you, with no fees or commissions.Get My Cash Offer →

Frequently asked questions

When did the Red River last set a record at Fargo?

The 2009 crest of 40.84 feet is the record, above the 1997 crest of 39.72 feet. Check the National Weather Service for current river data.

Do I need to pay off Fargo special assessments before selling?

Ask the Special Assessment Division at 701.241.1326 and your title company who carries the balance at sale. You can request a payoff amount through the city's form.

Who gets the Cass County tax bill in a sale?

Bills go to the owner of record as of November 1. Check the closing statement or ask your title company who pays which part of the year.

Does Fargo require a rental license?

Fargo asks owners to record rentals with the Inspections Department, which is free. Inspectors then check the property against the maintenance code.

Is a cash offer a good idea in Fargo?

It can be when the house needs repairs, is inherited or is a tenant-occupied rental. Compare it with listing costs and timing before you decide.

Selling in Bismarck: the lay of the land

North Dakota's capital city sits on the Missouri River's east bank, facing Mandan, and serves as the Burleigh County seat. Its 36.5 square miles rise to 1,745 feet. Median household income reached $73,877 in 2024, and the state government, Sanford Health and Bismarck Public Schools lead local hiring, so plenty of sellers are working around a job change or a retirement date.

Age separates one neighborhood from another, and buyers price accordingly:

  • Near downtown, the Cathedral District has homes dating to the 1880s and elm-lined streets.
  • The south side built up quickly after Garrison Dam improved flood control in 1953.
  • Newer growth runs north, near the shopping centers.

On the oldest blocks, you may find original plumbing, knob-and-tube wiring or tired foundations, and those repairs are what bog down an ordinary listing. Homes on the newer north and south edges more often carry special assessments for street and utility work.

Because Mandan is a short drive across the river but in Morton County, check the county and city of your parcel before searching for tax or permit records.

Winter and what buyers check

Winters in Bismarck are long, windy and snowy. January averages about 12.8 degrees Fahrenheit, the coldest reading on record is minus 45, and snowfall averages 50.5 inches a year. Roofs, furnaces and insulation take a beating season after season.

Expect inspectors to start with the roof, the furnace and the sump pump. An aging heater tends to lower offers. Seasonal flooding along the Upper Missouri continues, so a house close to the water should have its flood zone status checked ahead of a listing.

How special assessments work

Think of a special assessment as your share of a public improvement that serves your block. The owner of record pays it on the same bill as the property tax. City Engineering picks the project and splits the cost among the parcels that gain from it.

How your share is measured varies with the type of work:

  • Storm sewer is measured by the square footage of your lot.
  • Sewer and water follow the front footage of your lot.
  • Paving and street lights are a flat charge per parcel or lot.
  • Sidewalk, curb and gutter depend on how much was installed.

Owners may clear the whole amount or spread payments across three to 15 years, depending on the improvement. Each year's installment shows on the tax statement and is paid at the Burleigh County Auditor's Office. Ahead of closing, ask the county for what is left. A buyer or title company will want that balance cleared or assigned in the contract.

Free, no-obligation offerTell us about your Bismarck house and get a written cash offer within 24 hours.Get My Cash Offer →

Burleigh County tax dates

January 1 is the nominal due date, but most owners pay half on March 1 and half on October 15. Clearing the full amount by February 15 takes 5 percent off. Real property is valued as of February 1, and the county mails bills around December 26.

DateWhat happens
February 1Assessment date for real property
February 15Last day to pay in full and take the 5 percent discount
March 1First installment and special assessments due without penalty
April 1Deadline to apply for the Primary Residence Credit and homestead credit
October 15Second installment due without penalty

Payment options are the county website, the phone line at 1-800-272-9829, or a check mailed to PO Box 5518, Bismarck, ND 58506-5518. Anything mailed without a postmark by the due date is late. Cards come with a processing fee.

What a Bismarck seller must disclose

An owner of a home with four units or fewer has to reveal material facts, meaning anything that could meaningfully change how an ordinary buyer would use and enjoy the place. When an agent handles the sale, the disclosure goes on a written form in the Real Estate Commission's format, and the buyer must have it before accepting the final purchase agreement.

Century Code section 47-10-02.1 carves out exemptions: sales by a fiduciary managing an estate or trust, transfers among close relatives and foreclosure sales. That is why inherited houses often change hands with fewer formalities. The statute gives buyers no private claim, though an agent who ignores it can be disciplined by the Real Estate Commission.

Closing costs here also benefit from the absence of any deed or mortgage tax in North Dakota.

Your options for selling

Three paths lead to a sale: an agent, a private sale or a cash buyer. Each one costs you in time, price or certainty. Listing usually brings repair work, showings and a wait while the buyer's bank approves a loan.

  • An agent suits a house in solid shape when you can wait on a mortgage buyer.
  • A private sale suits you if a buyer is already found and the paperwork is no worry.
  • A cash offer suits a house that needs work, came through an estate, has tenants or faces a deadline.

Cash buyers take the house in its present state, so repairs and open houses come off your list. Whichever way you go, finish three tasks before picking a closing date:

  • Request a mortgage payoff statement.
  • Learn your special assessment balance.
  • Pull up the county tax record for this year.

Offers depend on the property, so we promise no price or timeline before seeing the house.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy Bismarck houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

Inherited a Bismarck house

Plenty of local sellers inherited a house and live somewhere else. Selling it as it is works fine. Bring together the death certificate, the county tax record and any special assessment balance, and see an attorney about probate before a deed gets signed. Estate fiduciaries skip the written disclosure form, so paperwork is lighter, but telling the buyer what you know is still the right move.

An empty house keeps costing money. Tax and assessment installments continue to come due, and the furnace has to run through winter to protect the pipes. A cash sale with a set closing date can end those costs sooner than a listing that waits for a mortgage buyer. Many heirs also find that a quick sale spares them repeated trips to manage repairs from far away.

A closing, step by step

The path is similar for nearly every sale in town. Terms are agreed, a title company opens a file, and it requests your payoff from the lender plus tax and special assessment figures from the Burleigh County Auditor. If anything does not add up, it surfaces at this stage. On closing day the title company retires the loan, clears tax and assessment balances out of your proceeds and gives you the remainder.

Timing the sale around the February 15 and March 1 dates can change what you owe, since the discount and the first installment both fall in that stretch. If the house closes shortly after a due date, check whether that installment has been paid so it is not counted twice.

Frequently asked questions

Is there a transfer tax on a Bismarck home sale?

Not from the state: North Dakota has no deed or mortgage tax. Federal income tax on any gain is a separate matter, so talk to a tax professional.

Who owes the Burleigh County tax in the year a house sells?

The statement is sent to the owner of record. The closing statement divides the year between buyer and seller, so ask your title company how it will handle that.

Can I sell a Bismarck house with special assessments still owing?

Yes. Installments run three to 15 years and appear on the tax statement. The balance is paid at closing, or the buyer carries it if the contract says so.

Do I have to fill out a seller disclosure in Bismarck?

With an agent, you need a written disclosure before the buyer signs the final acceptance. Without one, you still must disclose material facts in writing. Estates and some family transfers are exempt.

What should I do with an inherited Bismarck house?

You can sell it as it is. Gather the death certificate, the county tax record and any assessment balance, and ask an attorney about probate before signing a deed.

Selling in Grand Forks?

Selling a house in Grand Forks

The seat of Grand Forks County lies on the Red River of the North's western bank, just below the mouth of the Red Lake River. At 837 feet and about 29.3 square miles, it is 74 miles from Fargo-Moorhead and 145 miles from Winnipeg. Population went from 1,705 in 1880 to 59,166 in the 2020 census, thanks to early railroads and to the University of North Dakota, which opened in 1883. An Air Force base added thousands of jobs starting in 1954.

Education, defense and health care drive the economy here, so owners who rented to students, faculty or service members often sell after a tenant moves out, on a schedule they did not pick.

The 1997 flood and what it left behind

The April 1997 Red River flood devastated the city. It led to a new levee system and a greenway where homes once stood.

1997 flood measureFigure
Crest at East Grand Forks, April 2254.35 feet (flood stage 28 feet, 1979 record 48.8 feet)
Damage near Grand Forks and East Grand Forks$3.6 billion
Downtown buildings destroyed by fire, April 1911, including 60 apartments
Dike system cost, reported a decade later$400 million

Levees went up over the following decade, and many residents had to move. Where their homes stood is now the Greater Grand Forks Greenway. For a house close to the river, your insurer and the city can tell you its flood zone.

Before listing, look at the basement and the sump pump. A house that took on water in a recent spring should come with invoices and photos for the buyer.

Winter and what buyers check

Summers are warm and the climate is humid continental, yet freezing temperatures have been recorded in every month. Precipitation averages about 21.7 inches a year and snowfall about 48.4 inches, with extremes of minus 43 degrees Fahrenheit and 109. Because of that range, buyers study the roof, furnace and insulation.

A useful habit before listing: walk the house in the coldest part of the year, or picture it that way. Note where drafts come in, how the furnace sounds, and whether the attic is dry. Fixing a small problem, or at least disclosing it, usually costs less than a price cut after a buyer finds it.

Free, no-obligation offerTell us about your Grand Forks house and get a written cash offer within 24 hours.Get My Cash Offer →

Rental inspection rules

Every rental unit needs a Certificate of Occupancy here, rent charged or not, and since 2006 one- and two-family rentals have also needed a license. Each rental is inspected roughly every five years, with earlier visits after complaints.

What inspectors check:

  • Heat that holds every occupied room at 68 degrees, measured three feet above the floor
  • Two or more off-street parking spaces, scaled to bedroom count
  • Smoke detectors, egress, wiring and railings, judged by the code in force when the building went up
  • A cap of four unrelated people per unit
  • No junk or junk vehicles on the property when the certificate issues

An owner who ignores the rules can be cited in municipal court, and a judge may order the unit vacated. Selling a rental? Check the certificate first, because the buyer will want to see it.

The County Recorder's role in a sale

Any document that bears on title, a deed above all, is filed for good at the Grand Forks County Recorder's Office. Visit 151 South 4th Street or call 701-780-8262.

North Dakota levies no deed or mortgage tax, so none is due. Copies run $1.00 per page. A certified copy costs $5.00 for its first page and $2.00 for every page after. The office or your title company can quote recording fees.

Sellers of homes with as many as four units must list material facts in writing under state law. Not covered by that rule, per Century Code 47-10-02.1: sales by a mortgagor in default, foreclosure sales and transfers by estate fiduciaries.

Property taxes at sale

Statewide, a full real estate tax payment by February 15 earns 5 percent off, and the alternative is a pair of installments due March 1 and October 15. The Grand Forks County Treasurer can confirm what your parcel owes. The title company pays that from your proceeds when the sale closes, and a payoff dated for closing day avoids surprises.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy Grand Forks houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

Selling when you are behind on payments

You can sell at any point before a foreclosure sale, and the state's process leaves room to act. Lenders go through court, usually after 30 to 90 days' notice, and a borrower has 30 days from the notice to reinstate the loan.

Once a sale happens, redemption generally runs 60 days. No deficiency judgment is allowed on owner-occupied residential property of four or fewer units on up to 40 contiguous acres. Military families near the base also get added protection from the federal Servicemembers Civil Relief Act. An attorney can explain your options.

A cash offer is a quick route, since it buys the house as it stands. We promise no price before seeing it. Weigh it against listing, counting repairs, commissions and time.

What to line up before closing

Your take-home from a Grand Forks sale depends on three figures: what you owe the lender, what you owe the county in tax, and what the Recorder charges to file. Order each early, and ask for numbers that hold through closing day. For a rental, add the Certificate of Occupancy to the stack.

  • A payoff letter from your lender
  • A tax balance from the Grand Forks County Treasurer
  • The Certificate of Occupancy and any inspection history, if tenants live there
  • Flood insurance papers and flood zone details for a house near the river
  • Your deed, or estate papers if the house was inherited

Once these are in one folder, a buyer or title company can estimate your net within a day or two. That works the same way for a listing or a cash sale, and it spares you surprises at the closing table.

How a cash sale works here

Cash buyers purchase the house in its present state. Repairs, staging and open houses are off the table, and no lender appraisal comes between the offer and closing. That suits a house that needs work, a unit a tenant just left, or a deadline set by a military move or new job.

A title company still handles the paperwork. It checks title, gathers the tax and mortgage payoffs and pays them from your proceeds, and then the Recorder's Office files the deed. If the house has flood history, rental problems or deferred maintenance, a cash buyer prices those in from the start, so you do not negotiate repair requests after an inspection.

Compare any offer with the cost of listing: repairs, commissions and the months of carrying costs while you wait for a buyer's loan.

You pick the closing dateClose in as little as 7 days or on the date that works for you, with no fees or commissions.Get My Cash Offer →

Frequently asked questions

Can Grand Forks flood again?

Levees were finished roughly ten years after 1997, and the former floodplain is now the Greenway. For your own lot, ask the city and your insurer.

Do Grand Forks landlords need a license?

Since 2006, one- and two-family rentals have needed a license, and every rental needs a Certificate of Occupancy.

Will I owe a deed tax when my Grand Forks house sells?

No, because the state has no deed or mortgage tax. Recording and title fees are charged separately.

What if I fall behind on my Grand Forks mortgage?

Expect a lender's notice 30 to 90 days before a lawsuit, with 30 days to pay what is past due. A judge has to approve any foreclosure sale.

When do Grand Forks County property taxes come due?

Pay by February 15 for a 5 percent discount, or in installments on March 1 and October 15. The Treasurer can give you your balance.

Selling in Minot?

Minot at a glance

Minot is a north-central North Dakota city in Ward County, on the Drift Prairie roughly 110 miles north of Bismarck. About 47,308 people lived here as of July 1, 2025. The Mouse River, also called the Souris, cuts the city in half from west to east. Locals talk about three areas: North Hill on the plateau north of the valley, the river valley with downtown and the older neighborhoods beside the water, and South Hill across the south side.

US 2, US 52 and US 83 all meet here. Minot Air Force Base lies about 13 miles north, and the families connected to it are a steady source of housing demand. Homes in town range across more than a century of construction, so repair needs differ widely from one house to the next.

Mouse River flooding and your sale

The river is the biggest factor in how buyers and insurers view a property in or near the valley. A flood in April 1969 devastated the city, and the Army Corps of Engineers later straightened the channel and built flood control works.

The 2011 flood was larger. On June 26, 2011 the river crested at 1,561.7 feet, three feet above the record set in 1881. About 12,000 people were evacuated, more than 4,100 homes were affected, 2,376 of them extensively, and 805 were damaged beyond repair. The state's Department of Emergency Services reported that the old flood control system was built for flows up to 5,000 cubic feet per second, while the June 2011 flows topped 27,400.

  • The Mouse River Enhanced Flood Protection Project began in 2011 to cut flood risk across the basin.
  • FEMA has been developing new flood insurance rate maps for the Mouse River Basin since that flood.
  • Construction continues in downtown Minot under a phase labeled MI-6, along the east Central Avenue corridor.

If your house flooded, was repaired or was bought out, keep every record. Buyers will ask, and North Dakota's disclosure form covers latent defects, structural systems and environmental issues. The Mouse River Flood Protection Plan site has project updates and a flood insurance page.

Winter and what inspectors look at

Winters are long. Highs average 15 degrees and lows minus 2, and yearly snowfall runs 34 to 40 inches. Heating, insulation and roofing are the first systems a buyer's inspector checks.

  • Spring averages 51 for highs and 31 for lows, so repeated thaws and refreezes stress roofs, gutters and basements.
  • Ground squirrels are common in the inner city and can hollow out soil beneath structures, which is worth a look around the foundation.

Annual precipitation is 17.24 inches, and the climate is covered on the Minot Area Chamber EDC climate page.

Property tax billing and payment

Ward County sends the bills, using the state formula. Half of market value counts as assessed value, and a house's taxable share is 4.5 percent of true and full value. Whatever mills the taxing bodies on your parcel levy are applied to that.

Payment stepDate or contact
Tax dueThe January 1 following the assessment year
5 percent discountFull payment by February 15 (N.D.C.C. 57-20-09)
Penalty-free deadlineMarch 1
Valuation questionsWard County Tax Equalization office
AppealsState Property Tax division, 701-328-3127

Credits for a primary residence and for homestead appear on the state's residential property tax page. The county runs a property tax lookup and payment portal, and you can mail the Treasurer at PO Box 5005, Minot, ND 58702. Check your balance before signing a purchase agreement, since unpaid taxes and special assessments come out of your proceeds.

Permits, contractors and code violations

The city's Building Safety division enforces state and local rules on building and altering structures. Minot asks contractors in many trades to hold a city license on top of the state contractor registration, so confirm both licenses before hiring anyone for pre-sale fixes.

When the city corrects a code violation itself, the cost can be levied as a special assessment against the property, as a city ordinance item on the agenda center describes. An open complaint at a house you're selling can therefore turn into a balance that the buyer or title company wants cleared. Ask Building Safety what, if anything, is outstanding. The division's page is at minotnd.gov.

Chapter 5.5 of the city code bars permanent habitation in a camper vehicle in residential, commercial and industrial zones. The zoning ordinance defines temporary workforce housing separately, and the list of amendments shows moratoria on processing workforce housing applications and on tent structures. Read the code on the city's code site, or ask Planning and Zoning how your parcel is classified.

A deed can split the minerals from the surface, and North Dakota law sets default readings. Under N.D.C.C. 47-10-25, a surface deed signed on or after July 1, 1983 that reserves any minerals is treated as reserving every mineral of any kind unless some are excluded by name. Gravel, clay and scoria go with the surface unless the deed reserves them by name.

Section 47-10-24 works the other way for conveyances of mineral rights, reading them to convey all minerals except those specifically excluded by name. Wording decides everything here, so find your vesting deed and any earlier reservations before you agree on a price. A title company or attorney can confirm what you own, and that answer should be in hand before you list so buyers aren't left guessing. Both sections appear in the legislature's Title 47 chapter 10.

The town grew out of a railroad camp in 1878. Homes near the old center can be a century old, and newer subdivisions have far younger systems, so condition swings widely between neighboring streets. Inspectors spend the most time on wiring, plumbing and heat in the older blocks.

Winter wear and what inspectors check

Seasons here swing hard. January afternoons average about 22.5 degrees and nights about 2.7, which keeps a furnace running for months. Expect roof, heating and foundation to get the closest look from a buyer.

The city's building department treats furnace changeouts and water heater changeouts as permit jobs. If you swapped one out without a permit, the paperwork question will likely come up during inspection. Dig out receipts and permit records before listing.

Permits before a sale

Selling doesn't require a permit, but missing permits for past work tend to stall a Mandan deal once questions start. The Building Department (701-667-3230) wants a permit before work begins, noting that a construction record matters at sale, refinance or insurance time. The city's permit FAQ names these jobs:

  • any structural alteration, residential or commercial
  • residential construction over $2,000
  • window replacements that change the window size
  • any structure larger than 120 square feet
  • furnace changeouts, water heater changeouts and fireplace installs
  • water and sewer hookups

Painting, carpeting, tiling, countertops, fences up to 8.5 feet and swimming pools don't need one. A permit usually takes under an hour to issue, and inspections carry no extra charge. Verify a contractor's license with the state before paying for pre-sale repairs.

Special assessments when you sell

Cities bill nearby owners for public projects through special assessments, and any balance still owed stays with the property when it changes hands. Mandan uses assessments for street paving, water and sewer mains, sidewalks, curb and gutter, and also for weed cutting, snow removal and diseased tree removal.

On the city's special assessment page, water, sewer and street costs are generally spread over 15 years. Repairs to private water or sewer lines and tree removal are typically spread over five. Weed cutting and delinquent utility bills carry a 10 percent administrative fee. The city auditor certifies each year's installment to the county by November 1, and owners can pay without interest through February 15 of the following year.

  • Search an address or parcel on the city's Special Assessment Inquiry Dashboard. If the parcel doesn't appear, no specials are on it.
  • Call 701-667-3271 for payoff figures, or visit the Auditor's Office at 205 2nd Avenue NW.
  • For rural parcels outside city limits, Morton County handles balances at 701-667-3326.

Ask for a payoff figure first. That sum is taken from your proceeds when the sale closes.

Property tax dates and how the tax is figured

A Morton County bill starts with the assessor's market-based value. Half of it becomes assessed value, and a home's taxable value comes to 4.5 percent of the full figure. Mills levied by the city, school district and other local bodies are then applied. The State Tax Commissioner's residential property tax page explains each step.

A bill lost in the mail is still owed. The state's residential page lists credits for a primary residence and for homestead, and if you still qualify, claim one before you sell.

Before you list: a short checklist

A little preparation keeps a Mandan sale from stalling at the last step. Work through these in order.

  • Look up your parcel on the special assessment dashboard, and call the Auditor's Office if anything shows.
  • Find your latest tax statement and confirm whether the February 15 discount or the March 1 deadline is still ahead.
  • Gather permit records for any furnace, water heater, addition or structural work, and note anything done without one.
  • Locate any radon test results and, if you belong to an association, its documents and fee information.
  • Check that the name and mailing address on your deed are correct for the Recorder.

With those in hand, a title company can quote payoffs quickly and a buyer, cash or financed, has fewer reasons to pause.

Disclosure and recording

Before a buyer signs final acceptance, the seller of a one-to-four unit home gives a written statement of material facts (N.D.C.C. 47-10-02.1). Estate fiduciaries, foreclosure sales and close-family transfers are carved out.

  • Radon: section 47-10-02.2 has you state in writing what you know about radon levels and pass along any test or mitigation records.
  • Associations: section 47-10-02.3 sets ten days after signing for association documents and fee details.
  • Deeds: section 47-10-07 puts the mailing address of every grantee on the deed.

Your deed goes to the Morton County Recorder, whose land records feed the tax rolls. Owners can sign up there for a free Property Fraud Alert that flags any new recorded document. Read the statutes in the legislature's Title 47 chapter 10.

Frequently asked questions

Is Mandan the county seat of Morton County?

Yes, since 1881. The courthouse, Recorder, Treasurer and Tax Equalization offices all sit in town, so recording and tax questions stay local.

When are Mandan property taxes due?

Statements go out each December. Pay by February 15 for a 5 percent discount on the consolidated tax (a postmark counts), or by March 1 to avoid a penalty.

Is a permit needed to replace a furnace or water heater in Mandan?

Yes, both are on the city's permit list. For any other project, call the Building Department at 701-667-3230.

Who pays special assessments when a Mandan house is sold?

The contract decides, so get it in writing. The debt belongs to the parcel. The Auditor's Office at 701-667-3271 can give you a payoff figure before you accept an offer.

Must I give a buyer a disclosure statement?

In most sales of homes with up to four units, yes. The written statement is required by N.D.C.C. 47-10-02.1, with a radon statement added by 47-10-02.2. Estate fiduciaries, foreclosures and some family transfers skip the main form.
